# Mixed-fiber barycentric density selection in convex order

This note proves a mixed version of
`candidate 9c4bb3ca1bcd69e1`.
The density exponent is the continuous dimension d, not n+d. The
proof never assumes that a full-ambient exceptional null set misses a
sampled fiber. Its replacement is the pullback calculation in Section 3.
This theorem is not an OC depth bound.

## 1. Exact statement

Let n,d>=0, n+d>=1. For each i=1,...,k let P_i be a finite subset of
R^n and let gamma_i be a finite positive compactly supported Borel
measure on P_i times R^d. Suppose these measures have common mass M,
and let lambda_i>0 have sum one. Define the finite barycentric base set

    P=sum_i lambda_i P_i
      ={sum_i lambda_i p_i: p_i in P_i}.

For a finite base set Q, write

    sigma_Q=sum_(q in Q) delta_q tensor Leb_d.

When d=0, Leb_0 means mass one on the single point R^0, so sigma_Q is
counting measure on Q. When n=0 there is just one base point.

Assume gamma_i<=a_i sigma_Pi, where 0<a_i<infinity. For a coupling pi
of the gamma_i, let rho_pi be the pushforward by the full physical
barycentric map b(w_1,...,w_k)=sum_i lambda_i w_i.

**Theorem.** For every old coupling pi_0 there is a coupling pi of
the SAME marginals such that

    rho_pi0 <=_cx rho_pi,
    rho_pi <= A_d sigma_P,                         (1)

where convex order tests every finite convex function on R^(n+d), and

    A_d=(sum_i lambda_i a_i^(-1/d))^(-d),   d>=1,
    A_0=min_i a_i,                         d=0.    (2)

In particular, if a_i=1, the selected law has density at most one on
every output fiber, in every dimension including d=0.

If P_i are integer sets and P is a subset of Z^n, the output law is
supported on Z^n times R^d. The requirement concerns every base tuple
in the product, not only the tuples used by the old coupling. An
important instance is k=2, equal weights, and both P_i contained in
one common parity class modulo 2Z^n. More generally, equal weights
1/k and a common residue class modulo kZ^n suffice.

If M=0 all laws are zero. We assume M>0 in the proof. The case n=0
recovers the continuous theorem. No rationality of the finite base
sets is required for the measure statement itself.

## 2. The optimal full-ambient surplus and its inverse maps

Fix a smooth globally uniformly strongly convex function
phi:R^(n+d)->R. Maximize integral phi(b(w)) d pi over all couplings.
The compact dual attainment and separate global dual extensions proved
in Sections 2-3 of the continuous note apply without any absolute
continuity assumption. In detail, an attained compact dual tuple u_i
satisfies sum_i u_i(w_i)>=phi(b(w)), with equality on an optimal
coupling pi. The separate functions

    U_i(v)=max_(w_j in supp gamma_j, j!=i)
       [phi(lambda_i v+sum_(j!=i)lambda_j w_j)
                                         -sum_(j!=i)u_j(w_j)]

are finite and uniformly strongly convex on the FULL space R^(n+d).
At every equality tuple,

    lambda_i grad phi(b(w)) belongs to partial U_i(w_i).

Therefore, putting V_i=U_i^* and

    F_i(z)=grad V_i(lambda_i grad phi(z)),          (3)

one has w_i=F_i(b(w)) for pi-almost every tuple. Each grad V_i is
globally Lipschitz, and F_i is locally Lipschitz. Consequently, for
rho=b_*pi,

    (F_i)_*rho=gamma_i,
    sum_i lambda_i F_i(z)=z       rho-almost everywhere. (4)

We emphasize that these are full physical identities, including the
base coordinates. They do not change any integer label by a rounding
map. The inverse maps in (3) exist globally even though the marginals
are carried by finitely many lower-dimensional affine fibers.

## 3. Pullback lemma avoiding ambient Hessian exceptional sets

**Lemma.** Let V be a convex C^1 function on R^N with locally Lipschitz
gradient. Let q:Omega->R^N be C^2 on an open subset Omega of R^d, and
put F=grad V composed with q. Then F is locally Lipschitz and, for
Lebesgue-almost every y in Omega, the d by d matrix

    (Dq(y))^T DF(y)                                (5)

is symmetric positive semidefinite.

**Proof.** The C^1 function g=V composed with q satisfies

    grad g=(Dq)^T F.

This gradient is locally Lipschitz. Its weak Hessian is symmetric,
and at almost every point the ordinary derivatives of F and grad g
exist and agree with their weak derivatives. The product rule gives

    D^2 g=(Dq)^T DF+sum_(a=1)^N F_a D^2 q_a.

Every term in the sum is symmetric, so (5) is symmetric almost
everywhere. Monotonicity of grad V gives, for all sufficiently small h,

    [F(y+h)-F(y)].[q(y+h)-q(y)] >=0.

At any point where F is differentiable, substitute h=t v, divide by
t^2, and let t tend to zero. For every v this gives

    v^T (Dq)^T DF v >=0.

Together with symmetry, this is positive semidefiniteness. QED.

This argument takes derivatives in y directly. It does not restrict
an almost-everywhere ambient Hessian statement to a lower-dimensional
set, an operation that would in general be invalid. Smooth phi in
Section 2 makes the q used below C^2.

## 4. Fiber absolute continuity and the correct slice Jacobians

Assume d>=1. For p in P let rho_p be the measure of the output fiber
{p} times R^d, expressed in its continuous coordinate y. On that slice
write

    F_i(p,y)=(B_i^base(y), T_i(y)),

where the first component takes values in R^n and the second in R^d.
Both are locally Lipschitz. Let E_p be the compact support of rho_p.
By continuity, after discarding only equality tuples of zero mass in
Section 2 or equivalently using the support of an optimal coupling,
we have on E_p

    B_i^base(y) in P_i,
    sum_i lambda_i T_i(y)=y.                      (6)

One may instead take the closed subset where these identities hold;
it has full rho_p measure and leads to the same argument.

For a Borel A subset E_p, partition A by the finitely many values of
B_i^base. Let A_q={y in A: B_i^base(y)=q}, q in P_i. Equation (4),
the marginal density bound, and the Lipschitz area formula give

    rho_p(A_q)
       <= gamma_i({q} times T_i(A_q))
       <= a_i Leb_d(T_i(A_q))
       <= a_i integral_(A_q) |det DT_i(y)| dy.

As in the continuous proof, analytic images are measured in the
completed Borel measures. Summing the finite partition proves

    rho_p(A) <= a_i integral_A |det DT_i(y)| dy.    (7)

Hence rho_p=h_p dy is absolutely continuous and, for every i,

    h_p(y)<=a_i |det DT_i(y)|       almost everywhere on E_p. (8)

The partition into actual input bases is necessary here. Projecting
all input fibers onto their continuous coordinates and then bounding
the resulting density by a_i would be false in general.

Partition E_p further into the finitely many joint strata

    E_(p;q_1,...,q_k)
       ={y in E_p: B_i^base(y)=q_i for every i}.

At almost every Lebesgue density point of each such stratum all F_i
are differentiable in y. A locally Lipschitz function that is constant
on a set has zero derivative at almost every density point of that
set. Applying this to the base components, and differentiating the
second identity in (6) on the same stratum, gives

    D_y F_i(p,y)=(0, D T_i(y)),
    sum_i lambda_i D T_i(y)=I_d.                  (9)

Since the strata are finite and rho_p is absolutely continuous, these
relations hold rho_p-almost everywhere. The density-point derivative
fact is proved explicitly in Section 4 of the continuous note and
does not require that a stratum contain an open set.

## 5. Positive slice matrices and the exact density exponent d

Apply the pullback lemma with V=V_i and

    q_i(y)=lambda_i grad phi(p,y).

At the points of (9), set H=D^2_(yy) phi(p,y). This d by d principal
block of the full Hessian is positive definite. Equations (5) and (9)
say that

    (Dq_i)^T D_y F_i=lambda_i H D T_i             (10)

is symmetric positive semidefinite. The mixed Hessian blocks multiply
the zero base derivatives in (9), which is exactly why only H remains.
Consequently

    C_i=H^(1/2) D T_i H^(-1/2)
       =H^(-1/2)(H D T_i)H^(-1/2)                (11)

is symmetric positive semidefinite, with det C_i=det DT_i>=0. Also

    sum_i lambda_i C_i=I_d.                       (12)

Combine (8), (11), (12), and eigenvalue arithmetic-geometric means:

    h_p^(1/d) sum_i lambda_i a_i^(-1/d)
       <= sum_i lambda_i (det C_i)^(1/d)
       <= sum_i lambda_i tr(C_i)/d
        =1.

Thus h_p<=A_d. This holds on every output fiber p, and the number of
such fibers is finite. Every smooth strongly convex surplus optimizer
therefore satisfies rho<=A_d sigma_P with exactly the continuous
dimension d in (2).

## 6. Purely discrete case and simultaneous convex order

If d=0, the output support P is finite. Equation (4) means that all
tuples above a given output point p have the same ith endpoint F_i(p).
Consequently

    rho({p}) <= gamma_i({F_i(p)}) <= a_i

for every i. Thus rho<=min_i a_i sigma_P. No determinant, Lebesgue
density argument, or 0^0 convention is used in this case.

For every d, let D be the set of fixed-marginal couplings whose output
law is dominated by A_d sigma_P. It is compact and convex, since all
supports are fixed and compact and measure domination is weakly
closed. It is nonempty by maximizing a smooth strongly convex
surplus as above. For any finite convex function f on R^(n+d), smooth
convolution plus epsilon |z|^2 approximates f uniformly on the compact
output support. Its maximizing couplings belong to D, so passage to
the limit gives

    max_(pi in D) integral f d rho_pi
                  >= integral f d rho_pi0.

Finite-dimensional separation, with nonnegative multipliers for any
finite collection of convex tests, followed by the finite-intersection
property of compact D, now supplies one pi satisfying every convex
comparison simultaneously. This is exactly the fully proved argument
of Section 5 of the continuous note, with sigma_P replacing Lebesgue
measure. Mass and first moments are unchanged because the original
marginals and weights are unchanged. This proves (1).

## 7. Sharpness and actual mixed-integer geometry

For d>=1, put all input measures on one common base and use the
homothetic convex-body marginal example in Section 7 of the continuous
note, now in R^d. Every output law is supported on the corresponding
weighted homothetic body in that one output fiber. Its total mass
divided by its volume is exactly A_d, and the common-point coupling
attains it. Thus the universal constant in (2) cannot be lowered.
For d=0, take all marginals to be one common point mass of size
M=min_i a_i. Every output law has that same atom, proving sharpness
of A_0 as a universal upper bound.

Suppose C is any compact convex set in the original mixed ambient
space, and each gamma_i is supported on C intersect (P_i times R^d).
Every tuple barycenter of every coupling belongs to C by convexity.
If P is an integer set, the selected law is therefore supported on
the ACTUAL set C intersect (Z^n times R^d), with per-fiber density
bounded by A_d. In the equal-density parity-midpoint case, it is a
submeasure of ordinary mixed-integer volume on those fibers.

This supplies one convex-order improvement with a physical density
ceiling. It does not say that its barycenter is a mixed-integer point;
does not compare halfspace indicators by convex order; does not
preserve every old conditional branch; and does not bound the amount
of mass one can assign to a parity class in an OC argument. The case
where only the old coupling uses integer barycenters, but some other
product base tuples have noninteger barycenters, is not covered by
an assertion that the new law remains mixed-integer. Restricting the
optimization to such admissible tuples would need a different dual
extension argument and is not silently assumed here.

There is an exact obstruction to extending the density-one conclusion
to a union of parity classes while allowing only same-parity pairs.
For n=d=1 and equal midpoint weights, take gamma_1 to be unit Lebesgue
measure on each interval fiber at bases 0 and 1, and gamma_2 to be the
same at bases 2 and 1. Both have mass two and per-fiber density one.
If only same-parity endpoint pairs are allowed, the even pair has
midpoint base 1 and so does the odd pair. Every midpoint law is then
supported on the single fiber {1} times [0,1], with mass two. It cannot
be bounded by unit mixed-integer volume. Applying the theorem within
ONE fixed parity class is valid, but summing different such selections
can create overlapping output density. This exact obstruction was
identified by the independent density audit.

## 8. Audit targets

The new step beyond the continuous theorem is the pullback lemma and
its use on the finite joint base strata. The measure calculation first
proves intrinsic d-dimensional absolute continuity on each output
fiber. Only then are density points of those strata used to kill base
derivatives. Pullback Hessian symmetry is obtained intrinsically, not
by restricting a full-ambient null set. The same positive principal
Hessian block conjugates all continuous endpoint derivatives. These
facts yield the exact d-dimensional constant without a loss depending
on n or the number of fibers.
